result:
**Recommendation: REST** (JSON over HTTP, described with OpenAPI), unless your consumers are mostly rich client apps that need to fetch deeply nested, highly variable data shapes.

For a public API, the deciding factor is that you don't control the clients, and REST is cheaper to operate and easier to adopt under that condition.

| Concern | REST | GraphQL |
|---|---|---|
| Consumer onboarding | Anyone can `curl` it; every language and tool works | Needs a GraphQL client and schema knowledge |
| Caching | HTTP caching, CDNs and ETags work out of the box | Mostly POST to one endpoint; caching needs persisted queries or client-side work |
| Rate limiting and abuse | Per-endpoint limits are simple | Needs query cost analysis, depth limits and complexity budgets |
| Performance predictability | Each endpoint has a known cost | Arbitrary queries make N+1 and expensive joins your problem |
| Flexible data fetching | Over- and under-fetching; multiple round trips for nested data | Client asks for exactly what it needs in one request |
| Evolution | Versioning is explicit (and a chore) | Additive changes and field deprecation are smooth |
| Typing and docs | OpenAPI, with good codegen | Built-in schema and introspection, excellent tooling |
| Errors and monitoring | HTTP status codes work with standard tooling | Often 200 with errors in the body; needs GraphQL-aware tooling |

**Why REST wins here**
- **Lower barrier for third parties:** public API adoption depends on time-to-first-call, and REST needs no special tooling.
- **Easier to protect:** with unknown clients, GraphQL's flexibility becomes an attack surface you have to build cost-limiting for.
- **Free infrastructure:** CDN caching, gateways, logging and status-code monitoring all work without extra effort.

**Pick GraphQL instead if**
- Your main consumers are front-end or mobile apps with many different views over a highly relational data model.
- You expect clients to need very different slices of the same data, and round trips matter.
- You are willing to invest in query cost limiting, persisted queries and dataloaders from day one.

Most over-fetching complaints in REST can be handled with sparse fieldsets (`?fields=`) and `?include=` for related resources. If real demand for flexible querying appears later, you can add GraphQL as a layer over the REST API; going the other way is much harder.

If you tell me who the consumers are and what the data model looks like, I can firm this up.
